Part 4 / Evidence and maintenance

ND12

Visual documentation

Locate the boundary. Follow the mechanism. Inspect the evidence.

ND12 / Visual documentation

Contents

Visual documentation

A DS showcase must make two screens, a hinged body and a small set of physical interactions understandable before a reader studies the guide. It must also say what was actually recorded. A beautifully timed button press beside moving LCD pixels can suggest a causal relationship that the capture does not contain. Good visual documentation controls that interpretation as carefully as it controls framing.

This chapter uses the public repository at 61845372142b41992916f3732ea102cc0f4c8edf. It explains the existing workflow, not a new capture session. Private cartridges, videos, timing receipts and browser stores were not needed to write it and are not book inputs.

The README is a front page, not the entire manual

The repository's GIF-first policy is explicit and local to this project. The front page offers motion and short captions; setup, detailed controls, limitations and release evidence live in linked documentation. This division is especially useful for DS: a hinge sequence communicates articulation quickly, while the 30–180-degree limit, session-only lock and occlusion rules require prose that should not interrupt every animation.

The documentation chain therefore has different jobs. The README attracts and orients. The guide tells a player how to act. MEDIA.md establishes capture provenance and interpretation. Public TODOs retain causal failures, acceptance criteria and qualification boundaries. This engineering book explains why those choices exist. Copying all five layers into the front page would make each layer harder to maintain.

The approved DS logo is artwork, not a native-game screenshot. Likewise, an image of a rear emblem documents branding placement, not cartridge compatibility. Workstreams 92 and 99 concern DS visual identity; 95, 100 and 103 concern physical markings. Keeping those claims separate prevents an attractive identity treatment from becoming accidental runtime evidence. The controlling policy and current edition are recorded in MEDIA.md, opening edition.

Two timelines, one scene

The current edition records the selected DS opening for 90 native seconds, then excludes its first eight seconds. Native time begins at entry to EJS_onGameStart, after core/cartridge loading, not at page navigation and not at a later host-ready notification. The recorder intercepts the served

player source in an isolated browser context and captures the native canvas. The DS row explicitly selects 90 seconds and an eight-second trim. See native acquisition hook.

That recording then becomes a source for a second operation. openingReplay() serves private opening videos through intercepted browser routes, creates off-DOM video/canvas pairs, and exposes the DS canvas through an instance-specific source accessor. Browser actions still operate real scene controls; the screen image is supplied by the recording. Geometry, materials and lighting are not replaced with a composited illustration. The implementation boundary is explicit in the replay installation and receipt declaration.

Consequently, a DS button GIF establishes physical button travel while an untouched opening plays. A stylus GIF establishes pickup and scene tracing, not native touchscreen response to that trace. A lighting GIF establishes scene light changes with recorded LCD content. Those are useful, honest demonstrations. Calling them live game-input demonstrations would be false, even though the source pixels originally came from a running native core. Capture-only replay must not become a shipping-player fallback.

Why an earlier honest capture can still be superseded

Workstream 117 produced fresh DS and shared-lighting recordings. Its capture state was not fabricated, but the owner rejected the tutorial/menu screens and requested untouched openings throughout the README. Workstream 120 therefore replaced every scene GIF, including desk and lamp sequences, rather than fixing only the main DS introduction.

This distinction is a maintenance lesson: technical authenticity does not guarantee that a capture satisfies the requested editorial state. Keep the earlier edition labeled historical; do not silently reuse its native-input description for replacement replay footage. MEDIA.md explicitly separates the current opening edition from the superseded capture round.

Loading is another editorial hazard. Workstream 115 moves selection back to the physical DS immediately and supplies animated loading feedback before slow identification/startup finishes. A short loading clip is not a boot benchmark. Cutting before readiness is acceptable if the caption says the full boot takes longer; implying that a cartridge starts within the clip's duration is not. The same discipline applies to workstream 116: an upright lighting clip documents the real lamp-pool placement, not a new studio rig or a promise that metallic blue is invariant under warm light.

Reproducibility without publishing private inputs

Reproduction scripts belong in the repository; local source recordings, ROMs and detailed receipts do not. Environment variables choose authorized local sources, and the capture receipt records revision, viewport, clip boundaries, errors and replay observations. This chapter references those public mechanisms without opening private evidence or copying personal paths. A future maintainer must supply their own lawful inputs and explicit capture destination; reading these instructions does not authorize a new capture or publication.

capture-desk-showcase.mjs measures clip starts and durations and records LCD progress at their boundaries. Its DS Inspect sequence exercises body, hinge and lock controls; lighting sequences operate actual scene switches. The final receipt retains errors rather than treating an incomplete take as an ordinary clip. See clip bookkeeping, DS scene sequences and receipt output.

Encoding is receipt-driven, not a manually guessed crop. clips() rejects capture errors and missing durations, validates frame rate and palette size, then uses FFmpeg scaling, palette generation and Bayer dithering. Ordinary feature clips trim half a second from the tail. Complete showcases provide encodedDuration, bypass that trim and calculate the final GIF delay in centiseconds. The complete DS clip uses eight frames per second and 64 colors to retain all 82 seconds below the publication size limit. Reduced palette and frame rate are delivery tradeoffs, not higher-quality evidence. The encoder and complete-window recorder explain that distinction.

Four different kinds of evidence

Local integrity answers whether files decode, have expected dimensions, durations and loop flags, and differ across temporal samples. A changing sample does not show that every frame is correctly framed.

Bounded visual review answers whether inspected frames show the intended state. The recorded workflow caught an axolotl panel hiding its lamp and a settings sequence missing its drawer. Replacing those takes addressed specific observed failures, not every possible visual defect.

Hosted qualification answers whether the exact source passed its delivery gate. MEDIA.md records that the opening-media commit's Pages run failed an unchanged fullscreen case and skipped deployment, followed by a bounded fixture correction and successful later deployment. Public GIF byte checks were a separate result. A reachable GitHub image did not retroactively turn the failed Pages run green.

Human approval concerns whether the owner accepts the appearance and editorial choices. Neither an empty browser error array nor a successful deployment supplies that judgment. The historical successful run still retained 21 existing skipped browser scenarios; this chapter creates no new test result or compatibility claim. See the publication record.

ND12-W01 — Write the caption from the evidence

Suppose the selected artifact is ds-inspect.gif. First identify the demonstrated mechanism: body rotation, hinge change and pose locking. Next identify the LCD source: the current edition's replayed native opening. Finally identify the destination: animated repository page or first-frame book still.

A defensible caption is: “DS body and hinge inspection with a session pose lock; recorded opening on the LCDs.” In the book, append the first-frame limitation. Do not write “the game responds while the player folds the DS.” That sentence would require separate live native-input evidence.

ND12-R01 — Retry after the condition changes

Now assume the GIF is valid but a controls panel covers the lamp during the brightness change. Decoding it again cannot repair the composition. In an authorized future capture, dismiss or reposition the panel through the real UI, retake the affected sequence, then repeat temporal review and integrity checks. Do not paint over the panel or substitute a brighter render.

If publication alone fails, preserve the distinction: verify the exact source and delivery gate rather than recording replacement footage to fix an unrelated hosted assertion. The present chapter performs neither retry; it specifies the decision rule.

ND12-Q01 — Does the book still prove that the light followed the lamp?

Explained answer

ND12-A01

Back to question

No. One frame can show a lamp and an illuminated region together. Motion requires the original sequence or separate temporal evidence. The source also explains that the light is attached to the movable root, but source structure is not a substitute for human review of the animation.

Source trail and edition boundary

The relevant public records are 115: immediate loading, 116: upright lighting, 117: earlier fresh media and 120: replacement opening edition. They document intent and historical receipts, not newly reproduced results. The four GIF links across these two chapters reuse current DS/shared scene assets unchanged. No historical dirty PNG, new photograph, regenerated artwork or new game capture is part of this manuscript.

Part 4 / Evidence and maintenance

ND13

The maintainer field guide

Locate the boundary. Follow the mechanism. Inspect the evidence.

ND13 / The maintainer field guide

Contents

The maintainer field guide

Question: where should a maintainer start when the DS is wrong? Outcome: select a bounded investigation, preserve evidence and change the component that owns the failure instead of hiding the symptom.

Start with the visible contract

Record which cartridge or original fixture, which view, which input path and which source revision produced the failure. State whether the result was local, hosted CI or the actual deployed website. Do not start by editing a timeout or downgrading resolution.

A compact fault map

Symptom First owner to inspect Evidence that matters
Upload remains in toolsDsController.load orderingPlaying view and advancing loading LCD before a held ROM read resolves
First startup failsAdapter loader and launch callbacksVisible CDN/error message, cancellation and retry
One screen duplicates the otherdsScreenRegions, paintScreensNative dimensions and distinct actual upper/lower output
Quick tap disappearsDsTouchQueue, native frame pollingNative contact at the clicked pixel, not only a DOM event
Touch drifts after rotationtouchAt, camera/model transformsActual lower-LCD ray and native mark under the pointer
Direction releases too earlyAdapter source setsMixed keyboard/pointer ownership and final release
Progress does not persistDsSaveStore, persistCompleted transaction and matching runtime/ROM identity
Upright shell disappearsScene lamp target and playing poseShell pixels under the actual lamp, with readable LCDs retained
A stylus stays held after leavingCleanup and availability guardsRelease/cancel, hidden held clone and returned docked model

These are starting points, not a promise that every symptom has one cause. Inspect the actual source and existing assertions before changing ownership.

Run the smallest relevant command

The application requires Node 22 or newer and its existing locked dependencies. From the repository root:

npm run build
npm run check
node --test tests\unit\ds-cartridge.test.mjs tests\unit\ds-controls.test.mjs tests\unit\ds-touch.test.mjs

Build creates the allowlisted static preview. Check performs the repository's source checks. The selected unit files cover DS format/control/touch logic, not native game compatibility. Restore dependencies only when missing or after a dependency-manifest change.

The managed browser preview serves built dist; rebuild after source changes. Use a unique existing test name instead of a Windows file path interpreted as a regular expression. For example:

npx playwright test --grep "DS upload leaves the sidebar"

This is a reproduction recipe, not a claim that this book-authoring task reran application tests. Preserve the existing viewport, deadlines, workers/retries and quality settings unless a separately justified change requires them. A named skipped case is not newly passing because a grep selects it.

ND13-W01 - Change touch-edge rounding

First inspect dsTouchFromUv and its unit cases. Predict UV zero, UV one, mid-screen and nonfinite/out-of-range behavior. Then inspect adapter dispatchTouch: its combined-canvas pixel-center rule is a second transformation, not a duplicate of the first.

Run focused unit cases, then the native pointer scenarios needed by the change: quick tap, held pen, changed orientation, zoom and high-DPI touch. Record any parked cases explicitly. A center-point screenshot alone cannot qualify an edge-rounding change.

Keep current guides current; keep editions historical

The player guide answers how to operate the current console. Architecture describes current boundaries. Verification records identified observations. The development ledger explains decisions and failed approaches. Numbered workstreams describe a finite outcome, its evidence and actual remaining work. This book explains the cutoff implementation in a coherent narrative.

When behavior changes, update the current guide and affected explanation, then create a clearly identified new rendered edition when necessary. Do not silently overwrite the original GBA book or re-label this edition's historical source pin. Keep the root README short and visual, linking readers to the detailed documentation.

ND13-R01 - A documentation-only correction

If only a caption or prose claim changes, inspect its source and rerun the documentation/book gates affected by the edit. Do not recapture every GIF or run unrelated native suites merely to make the change look rigorous. If the book builder changes, its own tests and actual rendered output are relevant; parser success alone is not layout review.

ND13-Q01 - When is the workstream complete?

Explained answer

ND13-A01 - When the promised outcome has its own evidence

Back to question

Implementation, targeted validation, documentation and owned continuity must agree. Where publication is authorized, verify the exact remote revision and artifact rather than assuming a push deployed it. Mirror the actual workstream in its issue and Project item. Keep human

acceptance, remaining compatibility limits and parked tests explicit instead of using one DONE label to imply all of them.

Source trail

Declared application commands. DS browser assertions. Touch queue unit evidence. Bounded parked-case record.

Source register and edition limits

What is pinned

Implementation and historical citations point to public repository revision 61845372142b41992916f3732ea102cc0f4c8edf. This is the runtime cutoff, not the later commit that publishes this book. The production source manifest hashes the actual manuscript, selected illustrations and builder inputs. It also records the pinned source files referenced by chapters.

The book synthesizes source-backed behavior and a selected causal history. It is not a complete export of every workstream, issue, transcript or development record. No private conversation or context store is a source. Unfinished historical states remain unfinished in the original records; later public qualification is described separately.

Included illustrations

The cover reuses supplied assets/ds-logo.png without regeneration. Four chapter figures select existing ds-inspect.gif, ds-lighting.gif, ds-gameplay.gif and axolotl-movement.gif. Print and offline HTML embed metadata-clean frame-zero PNG derivatives. This makes the reader independent of animation playback and the network; it also means a still cannot establish motion, a complete lighting comparison or an actual gameplay response.

The animated source remains available in the repository. Game output is historical showcase footage with recorded native LCD replay. No ROM, raw video or private filesystem path is embedded. The project notices remain the artwork/dependency provenance reference. This edition does not assert new ownership of supplied logos, game imagery or Nintendo marks.

Reproducibility and review boundary

The repository's locked local book dependencies render Mermaid and paginate with Chromium and Paged.js. PyMuPDF checks the real PDF. Installed system fonts and browser versions can affect pagination and bytes; a fresh-machine or byte-identical rebuild is not claimed.

Native text coverage, page geometry, link destinations, bookmarks and embedded fonts are mechanical checks. Contact sheets and selected larger native pages are a separate bounded visual review. Neither is user approval, PDF/UA conformance, printer prepress, a rights audit or new device testing. The production/review record names the exact delivered edition and limits.
